instructions:
You are reading the plain-language text of a codebase map. A reader meets each field ALONE, inside one box, with no paragraph around it, and does not read code.

Judge ONLY these two things:
  1. UNKNOWN WORD — a term the reader has not met and the field does not explain. Product words and words already in the map's Glossary are fine; jargon, an internal codename, or an unexplained abbreviation is not.
  2. LOST PRECISION — the sentence is short and plain but says nothing specific. "The system checks the user" is the shape: grammatical, readable, and it names no decision, no data and no actor. This is the worse failure, because it looks correct.

Do NOT report sentence length, em dashes, code names or an opening "It" — those are counted deterministically and the lead already has the numbers.
Be conservative. Report a field only when you can say WHICH word is unknown, or WHAT the sentence should have said. If in doubt, pass the field.

For each field you flag, return its `where` exactly as given, one of `unknown word` or `lost precision`, and one short line naming the word or the missing specific.

fields.text: A map that grew is never marked down for growing, because only lost content breaches an allowance.
A finer map would be reported as a step backwards, which teaches everyone to keep the map coarse.
Losing a check the accepted map passed blocks the run. A number that moved too far only asks for a human look.
Blocking on every wander would fail honest rebuilds, and everyone would stop reading the verdict.
How many boxes a map should hold is worked out from the code, never from the accepted map.
An accepted map drawn at the wrong zoom would set the target forever, so every rebuild repeats its mistake.
A run that cannot get one of the two sides refuses to report, instead of reporting that nothing got worse.
A quiet skip reads as a clean result. A run that compared nothing then looks like a run that found nothing.
A map edited after it was frozen cannot be scored, so the run stops on any later change to it.
Anyone could nudge a map until its score improved, and the report would look exactly the same.
A claim is settled only when most reviewers gave the same answer. A split with no majority stays unsettled.
A tie credited to one side turns an open disagreement into a fact the map presents as checked.
A reviewer answers holds up, disproved, or cannot tell. Any other word is refused rather than counted.
An unrecognised word quietly folded into a bucket credits an outcome nobody voted for.
A claim counts as challenged only when a reviewer voted on it.
Counting a claim as checked because it was handed out inflates how verified the map looks.
A pass that leaves claims unvoted is refused unless someone declares that stopping early was deliberate. The declaration must say which claims were prioritized.
An undeclared gap reads as a finished check, so nobody learns that a thousand claims went unread.
A pass that checked only part of the map still records the size of the whole claim surface.
Recording the smaller number lets a pass over a fifth of the map ship looking complete.
A vote about a claim missing from the list captured for the reviewers is refused.
A record built against a later snapshot describes a check that never happened on the map being shipped.
A build stops when the map still carries a claim its reviewers disproved, word for word.
Reducing a whole pass to counts hides a wrong claim, because a correction and an ignored refutation look the same.
A file cited as evidence that the reviewer's own record never names fails the check. A file it only saw printed by a search is flagged, not failed.
A check that fails honest reading teaches the next reviewer to hide how it read.
Every screen of the map should hold between three and nine boxes. Five is the number it aims for.
A screen packed with boxes buries the product, so the reader stops drilling and never finds what it does.
A screen whose boxes are all the same kind reads as a list, so fifteen boxes are fine there.
Cutting a plain list into invented groups adds levels that name nothing a reader was looking for.
Only the first screen is faulted for holding too few boxes. A screen deeper down may be small.
A first screen of two boxes tells the reader the technology used, never what the product does.
A group holding exactly one thing is reported, because that level costs a click and adds no meaning.
Wrapper levels push what the reader came for one click further down for nothing in return.
A crowded or thin screen is only ever advice. It never refuses a map or stops a build.
Refusing a map over a box count pushes a builder to invent groups that fit the number.
Regrouping may only move boxes between groups. It may never merge or split the boxes themselves.
Merging boxes to fix a crowded screen makes the map say the code holds fewer parts than it does.
A group is never one end of an arrow, so moving a box into another group moves no arrow.
An arrow leaving a whole group cannot be drawn on any one screen, so the picture stops making sense.
